jsnvu6-d1e1815-d1e106.summary: Rubric heading for Question 2, stating the question to be treated—whether God is everywhere—and cross-referencing the parallel treatment in Aquinas, Summa Theologiae I, q.8, a.2.
concepts: cross-reference to Aquinas ST I q.8 a.2

jsnvu6-d1e1815-d1e115.summary: Objection against divine ubiquity: permanent things relate to place as successive things relate to time; but in successive things one indivisible cannot be in diverse times at once; therefore a permanent indivisible, such as God, cannot be simultaneously in diverse places, and so God is not everywhere.
claims: Permanent things relate to place as successive things relate to time
An indivisible within a successive series cannot exist in diverse times simultaneously
Therefore a permanent indivisible such as God cannot be simultaneously in diverse places, and so is not everywhere

jsnvu6-d1e1815-d1e133.summary: Sed contra: God is in all things; every place is itself some thing; therefore God is in every place.
claims: God is in all things
Every place is itself a thing
Therefore God is in every place

jsnvu6-d1e1815-d1e143.summary: Responsio: place can be considered in two ways—as a created thing, in which sense God is in all places just as he is in all things; or as that which contains what is located, in which sense God in himself is nowhere, since he is contained by nothing but rather contains and conserves everything, while according to his effects he is everywhere, because he fills every place with them. This latter sense is the proper meaning of God's being everywhere, since nothing but God fills every place with its goodness and effects.
claims: Considered as a created thing, place is such that God is in every place, as he is in every thing
Considered as a container of what is located, God in himself is nowhere (being contained by nothing) but is everywhere according to his effects, which fill every place
Only God fills every place with his goodness and effects, which is the proper sense of divine ubiquity
concepts: place as created thing versus place as container
presence by effect versus presence in se

jsnvu6-d1e1815-d1e172.summary: Notes that the Master (Peter Lombard), in the text, distinguishes a threefold mode of being in place: circumscriptively, which belongs only to bodies whose outer boundary is measured by the ultimate boundary of the containing place; and definitively, which, as some say, belongs to created spiritual substances (to be inquired into shortly)—setting up discussion of a third mode.
claims: Peter Lombard distinguishes a threefold mode of being in place
Circumscriptive presence belongs only to bodies, measured by the limit of the containing place
Definitive presence is held by some to belong to created spiritual substances

jsnvu6-d1e1815-d1e192.summary: Neither of these two modes belongs to God: the circumscriptive mode implies limitation of corporeal quantity, and the definitive mode, according to those who posit it, implies limitation of essence and power—both repugnant to God. Moreover, by neither mode can anything be in several places at once, much less everywhere, since limitation by quantity of mass or of power prevents it, as held by those who say spirits are defined by place.
claims: The circumscriptive mode implies limitation of corporeal quantity and so is repugnant to God
The definitive mode, as its proponents hold it, implies limitation of essence and power and so is likewise repugnant to God
Neither mode permits something to be in several places at once, and so neither could account for God being everywhere
concepts: critique of circumscriptive and definitive presence as applied to God

jsnvu6-d1e1815-d1e216.summary: The third mode of being in place, namely repletively (by filling), belongs to God—not according to himself, but according to his effects, as already said—and so it is proper to God to be everywhere, since only divine power extends to producing all things existing or possible in place, that is, to filling place with effects. Being everywhere in this mode belongs to God not from eternity but in time, just as does producing the things by which every place is filled.
claims: The repletive mode of being in place—filling place with effects—belongs properly to God
Only divine power extends to producing all actual or possible things in place, which is what filling place with effects consists in
God's being everywhere in this repletive sense begins in time, coinciding with the production of the things that fill place, rather than holding from eternity

jsnvu6-d1e1815-d1e236.summary: Reply to the opening argument: just as among successive things there is an indivisible belonging to the successive series itself (like the 'now' or an instant of change), which cannot exist in several parts of time or motion, and another indivisible not of the successive genus (like eternity or aevum), which can coexist with the whole succession of motion or time—so too among quantities there is an indivisible belonging to quantity (like a point), which cannot be in several parts of magnitude or in several places, and another indivisible entirely outside the nature of corporeal quantity (like God), to which nothing prevents being present to all places and all things at once.
claims: An indivisible internal to a successive or quantitative series (a 'now', a point) cannot exist in several parts of that series at once
An indivisible outside that genus entirely (eternity/aevum with respect to time; God with respect to corporeal quantity) can coexist with the whole series
Therefore nothing prevents God, as an indivisible wholly outside corporeal quantity, from being present to all places at once
concepts: indivisibility within versus outside a genus

jsnvu6-d1e1815.summary: Question 2 asks whether God is everywhere. An objection argues that, since permanent things relate to place as successive things relate to time, and a successive indivisible cannot exist in diverse times at once, a permanent indivisible like God cannot be simultaneously in diverse places. The sed contra counters that since God is in all things and every place is itself a thing, God is in every place. The responsio distinguishes two senses of place: as a created thing (in which God is in every place, as in every thing) and as a container of what is located (in which God in himself is nowhere, being contained by nothing, but is everywhere according to his effects, which fill every place). This grounds a review of the Lombard's threefold mode of being in place—circumscriptive (proper to bodies), definitive (proper to created spirits)—both rejected as implying limitation inapplicable to God—and repletive (filling place with effects), which alone belongs properly to God, and which holds not from eternity but from the time God begins producing things. The reply to the opening objection resolves it by distinguishing indivisibles internal to a successive or quantitative series, which cannot be multiply located, from an indivisible wholly outside corporeal quantity, like God, to which no such restriction applies.
claims: God is everywhere in the proper sense of repletive presence: filling every place with his effects, while in himself being contained by no place
The circumscriptive and definitive modes of presence in place are repugnant to God because they entail limitation of quantity or of essence and power
God's universal presence in place is not eternal but begins with his producing the things that fill place
God's capacity to be wholly present in many places at once is intelligible because he is an indivisible entirely outside the genus of corporeal quantity, unlike a point or any successive indivisible
concepts: modes of being in place (circumscriptive, definitive, repletive)
presence by effect versus presence in se
